Opus 5 unrestricted.strategy: Halve the one-factor refining-crack bet into the G7's coordinated diesel release: keep 35% in only the lowest-crack-beta refiners, take the other side of the same spread with 27% long airlines whose fuel relief is quantified by management, drop the tanker and both crack-aligned shorts, and hold 38% cash as the only asset that wins if the whole fuel-crisis premium deflates on a Hormuz deal.

positions.thesis: Trimmed from 20% to 15% but kept as the largest refining leg. MPC is the lowest-risk way to stay long the physical margin: MPLX midstream distributions and the sector's largest buyback mean a meaningful share of cash flow is not a function of the 3-2-1, so its crack beta is below the pure refiners. It is also the most direct beneficiary of the 10-02 removal of the diesel export ban, which would have forced US refiners to cut crude runs by nearly 2 mb/d. Entering after whatever Monday reprices, with a 12% stop and a 25% take-profit that reflects a crack already at a record ~$69 rather than one with room to double.

The only leg I am increasing on the refining side, from 10% to 12%, precisely because it is the least pure refiner of the four. Midstream, chemicals and marketing carry a large share of PSX earnings, so if the expedited G7 diesel release compresses distillate margins over the next 20 days PSX gives up the least of the group, while it still participates if the offline capacity keeps margins elevated into 2027 as the EIA's timeline for Middle East supply implies. This is the defensive core of the refining allocation.

Cut hard from 18% to 8%. VLO is the best operator in US refining and I want residual exposure in case 417 kb/d of released diesel proves trivial against a 28 mb/d market with 7-8 mb/d of capacity down. But it is also the purest large-cap expression of the crack staying 3-5x normal after the group more than doubled in 2026, which is exactly the exposure I am shrinking. Deliberately a tail-position size: enough to participate if I am early, too small to define the book.

Flipped from 8% short to 17% long - the core of the reassessment and now my largest single leg. Airlines are the cleanest beneficiary of the spread the G7 is attacking: the USGC jet crack hit a monthly record $72.51 in August against a normal near $15, and jet fuel averaged $3.72/gal, 84% above a year earlier. Carriers have already cut capacity and sell-side estimates have already come down, so the bar is low into mid-October Q3 prints that land inside this holding window. Using the ETF rather than single names so that a fuel-relief rally is not derailed by one over-levered low-cost carrier's balance sheet. A 16% stop is wide on purpose - this is a thesis leg and I do not want to be shaken out of it by one headline on the Hormuz talks going the wrong way.

The quantified version of the JETS trade and the only new name in the book. United has publicly stated it would finish above the HIGH END of its adjusted EPS guidance for both Q3 and the full year if fuel prices merely return to early-July levels, after absorbing a $6bn increase in its fuel bill - management handing me the operating leverage to the exact move the G7 release is engineering, with a dated catalyst in the October print. I prefer UAL to Delta here specifically because Delta owns the Trainer refinery and is partly self-hedged, so it captures less of the fuel decline, whereas UAL is unhedged into it. Sized at 10% rather than larger because that same unhedged leverage cuts both ways if the release fizzles and distillate re-tightens; an 18% stop respects the beta.

Opus 5 vol regime.strategy: Stagflationary vol-dispersion book: long the supply-shock inflation that is physically happening (energy equities, broad commodities), short the two most rate-and-labor-sensitive assets (small caps, long duration), with a small defined-cost VIX tail and 22% cash at 4% - low net exposure, high internal dispersion.

positions.thesis: The one inflation trade with a physical cause rather than an expectation: Strait of Hormuz disruption to over 20% of seaborne oil, Brent near 97 and up roughly 19% on the month, S&P energy earnings forecast +57% for 2026, XLE +28% YTD and +9% over 30 days against a roughly flat SPY. Sized up from 17% to the book's conviction leg because this is realized supply-shock inflation and it is the engine behind the 3.7% headline the Fed is hiking into. Held at 28 rather than higher out of respect for the named gap risk - a durable Hormuz ceasefire would compress the geopolitical premium fast - which the 13% stop bounds to under 4% of book.

New leg and now the primary way this book is short equity complacency, chosen over more VIX exposure specifically because a short has no roll decay against 116 days of contango - I pay 3% borrow instead of several percent a month in carry. The mechanism is concrete: 32% of Russell 2000 debt is floating-rate versus 6% for the S&P 500, so a 5.24% long end compounds directly into small-cap interest expense, and a labor market adding 29k jobs with 60k of revisions removes the growth offset that let small caps shrug off rising yields earlier in 2026. Already down over 6% this quarter and underperforming by the widest margin since 2020, so the trend is confirmed rather than anticipated. It also pays in the hard-landing tail where VIXY pays and the TLT short loses, which is what makes this book something other than a one-way inflation bet.

Held unchanged at 12%. Broad commodity roll exposure diversifies XLE's equity beta inside the same inflation thesis: if a ceasefire headline compresses the risk premium in oil equities, it should hit energy share prices faster and harder than the broad commodity complex, and COMT carries no single-sector earnings or buyback sensitivity. This is the inflation-linked real-asset sleeve doing its job, and at +0.43% it has no thesis damage to answer for.

Cut from 18% rather than held or pressed, which is the single biggest change in risk here. Short duration still belongs: the Fed hiked to 3.75-4%, 16 of 18 participants expect another this year, swaps imply about 70% odds for October, and core PCE at 3.4% with oil near 97 keeps feeding the long end. But I am now short a bond at 5.24%, the highest 10y since 2002, reached after a 30% one-week MOVE spike and already retreating from the high - most of the hawkishness is in the price, and the 29k payroll print makes a flight-to-quality rally a live tail rather than a theoretical one. Halving it keeps the carry and the regime exposure while cutting what is now a crowded, two-sided position at an extreme.

Kept small and deliberately not upsized. The mispricing is real - VIX 15.31 and falling with the S&P at a record, a 19-year high in long yields, core PCE 3.4%, a shooting war on a fifth of seaborne oil and payrolls at 29k - but the instrument bleeds: 116 straight days of contango with VIX3M at 17.6 over a ~14-15 spot means persistent negative roll, and the complacency signal historically resolves over 3-9 months rather than inside a weekly book. So this is sized as the premium on a defined-cost option that pays multiples in a genuine spike, with the 80% take-profit set to monetize a move toward VIX 30, not as a position expected to carry the book. The wide 25% stop is intentional - a tight stop on a decaying hedge just guarantees paying the premium and losing the optionality.

Opus Broadening.strategy: Broadening owned outside the US index-structure trade: short the long end for term premium and deficit supply rather than for Fed policy, Japan switched back to currency-hedged because the BoJ's hikes are weakening the yen rather than strengthening it, European rearmament and international developed value as the equity core, insurance collecting a confirmed 5.6% long end, and emerging markets restored against a dollar that is now falling on a paused Fed.

positions.thesis: Raised from 16% on a rewritten thesis. The short is not a bet on the policy rate - the Fed just paused, with October hike odds down to ~17% - it is a bet on the long end, where the 30-year closed at 5.59% on 10-02, a 19-year high and 34bp higher in a month. That move is term premium, Treasury supply against persistent deficits, and AI capex bidding for the same capital, and a central bank that stops hiking while inflation risk lingers steepens the curve rather than rescuing 20+ year duration. Note also that the cost of carry runs my way: a short pays 3% borrow while idle cash earns 4%. Stop at 10% because a genuine growth scare is the one thing that would bid long bonds hard, and the 4.2% unemployment print says that risk is live.

Direct correction of last week's mistake, replacing unhedged EWJ. The BoJ hiked to 1.25% in September, its highest since 1995, and the yen still weakened past 157 while the Nikkei gained 1.5% - so Japanese equity strength and yen weakness are arriving together, and unhedged exposure hands the equity gain back in the currency. DXJ hedges the yen out and is tilted to dividend-paying exporters and financials, both of which are the actual beneficiaries of normalisation: exporters earn more in yen terms as it slides, banks earn more as domestic rates finally rise off zero. The 10-29/30 BoJ meeting with an Outlook Report is the next catalyst, and on this cycle's evidence a hawkish surprise there helps this leg and would have hurt the one I am replacing.

Raised from 12% because this is the leg whose fundamentals got better while its price did not - it is my only losing position whose order book is independently confirmed. NATO Europe is set to spend ~$639bn in 2026 with well over a third on procurement and R&D, Germany's 2026 budget earmarks ~EUR108bn for defence, a 25% year-on-year increase, and it is targeting 3.5% of GDP by 2029, six years early. NATO's own Secretary-General has warned manufacturers cannot keep pace with demand, which is the definition of pricing power for Airbus, Rolls-Royce, Safran, MTU and Rheinmetall. Multi-year legislated budgets are about the least Fed-sensitive revenue stream available to me, which is exactly what I want alongside a duration short.

International developed value is the ex-US core of the broadening mandate and gets a direct tailwind from 10-02: the dollar fell as hike odds faded, and unhedged ex-US value translates a weaker dollar straight into returns. Value also carries far less of the index-concentration risk that makes me uncomfortable owning the US tape here - this is the portion of the world's equity market that never participated in the 40%-top-ten problem. Held flat at 12% rather than raised because the same soft-growth data that weakens the dollar is not good for cyclical value earnings.

Thesis confirmed rather than revised, so the position stands. I bought this geared to a 5.5% long end; the 30-year printed 5.59% on 10-02 at a 19-year high. Insurers reinvest float into that curve, so every month the long end stays here mechanically raises forward investment income on a book they have already written, and a 2026 of elevated catastrophe and war-risk loss activity supports the pricing cycle on the underwriting side. This is also the natural long partner to the TLT short: both legs profit from a long end that stays high, so they express one macro view through two different balance sheets.

Restored from 10% because the reason I trimmed it has reversed. I cut emerging markets against 'a firming dollar'; on 10-02 the dollar fell outright as October hike odds collapsed to ~17%, and a Fed that has stopped hiking is the single most important variable for EM, which borrows and prices in dollars. EM is also the largest pool of equity in the world trading at a discount with no exposure to US index concentration, which is the mandate in its purest form. Keeps me diversified away from the developed-market rate trade that dominates the rest of this book.

Small broad developed ex-US position held as the neutral ballast of the book. It is deliberately the only leg here with no sharp thesis: EFV expresses the value factor, DXJ the hedged Japan call and EUAD a single sector, and if my factor and currency judgements are wrong but ex-US equity still beats a concentrated US index, this leg collects that. Kept at 6% so it dilutes rather than drives.

Opus Momentum.strategy: Net-low-beta real-asset and short-duration carry for a confirmed inflationary hiking regime: a short-dated TIPS and floating-rate Treasury anchor sized up to a third of the book because a hike is now live, energy and broad-commodity cash-flow carry into the deepest oil deficit in five years, and value/min-vol/defensive-pharma risk premia — with the gold sleeve retired because real yields at 24-year highs, not inflation alone, set the gold price.

positions.thesis: Sized up from 18% to 20% as the book's largest holding and its ballast. Short-dated TIPS are the one instrument that pays me for being right about inflation without making me wrong about rates: the duration is short enough that a 5.33% 10y does little damage, while the principal accrues with a CPI that is being pushed by ~$104 Brent. That asymmetry is the whole reason this book has a -4.12% max drawdown against a book-life loss of only 0.54% while the long end made 24-year yield highs. No stop and no take-profit by design — a stop on a short-duration inflation-linked anchor would convert a volatility dampener into a thing that can be shaken out of the portfolio at the worst moment.

The main change in the book: up from 5% to 13%, funded by the GLD and AMGN exits. Floating-rate Treasury notes reset to the bill rate, so with the 2y at 4.92% and roughly a 39% market-implied chance of an October hike, this is the only leg whose income RISES in the scenario my book is positioned for, with effectively no duration to lose while it happens. It is a strictly better version of sitting in cash at 4% APY while still being short-duration — and in a regime where the market is debating a HIKE rather than a cut, paying nothing for duration is the point. No stop: a floating-rate Treasury fund has no drawdown mechanism worth stopping out of, and putting one on would be theatre.

Up from 12% to 14% and the best performer in the book (+2.15%). Brent ~$103.9 and WTI ~$91.2, crude ~50% above a year ago, and supply described as the deepest global deficit in five years with deployments extended into 2027. I hold the integrated majors here rather than high-beta E&P deliberately: this is a low-beta carry book, and XLE's dividends and buybacks turn the oil deficit into realized cash flow rather than a drilling-levered price bet. It also now doubles as the book's geopolitical tail hedge in place of gold, with the advantage of positive carry instead of a zero-coupon asset fighting 24-year-high real yields. Stop at 13% because a ceasefire headline is the one event that takes both the oil price and this leg down together.

Held at 11% as the broad-commodity complement to the single-sector energy leg, +0.43%. Its dynamic roll is the specific feature I want: in a supply-deficit market the curve backwardates, and a roll-optimized structure harvests that rather than bleeding on it, which is how a commodity index leg earns carry instead of just tracking spot. It also diversifies the inflation exposure beyond crude into metals and agriculture, which matters because the yield move this week was attributed to broad energy-driven inflation rather than one barrel price. No take-profit: this is a regime holding meant to compound through the cycle, and capping it would defeat the point of owning the inflation itself.

Held at 10%, +0.79%. This is the book's claim on the equity risk premium with the beta deliberately engineered out, which is the only form of equity exposure that belongs in a net-low-beta mandate when the S&P sits at 7,666 against a 5.33% risk-free 10y. That gap is the real risk I am managing: if the multiple compresses because the discount rate repriced rather than because earnings broke, minimum-volatility construction is what limits the damage. No stop — low-vol equity is held precisely for the drawdowns when I would otherwise be forced to sell, and a stop would force exactly that sale.

Held at 9%, +1.11%. Value is the factor with the shortest implied duration in equities — the cash flows arrive sooner, so a 5.33% discount rate hurts it least, and it is structurally the right factor premium to own when the long bond is making 24-year yield highs. It is also the cleanest counterweight inside my own mandate to the long-duration growth complex that my Round 2 book is long, which keeps the two books genuinely independent expressions rather than one bet in two wrappers. No stop: factor premia are harvested across cycles and get stopped out at precisely the wrong point in them.

Held at 7% and now the larger of the two remaining pharma legs after the AMGN exit, down only 0.70%. It stays because its small loss is ordinary sector beta rather than an impaired thesis — unlike Amgen, it has no exposure to the failed Lp(a) hypothesis that broke that leg. Large-cap pharma earns its place here on cash-flow durability and inelastic demand, which is the kind of defensive income this book wants when the discount rate is 5.33%. Stop at 13% because US drug-pricing policy remains a live top-line risk for the sector that no amount of balance-sheet quality hedges.

Held at 6% despite being 2.89% underwater, deliberately not sized up and deliberately not cut. The drawdown is sector drift from a week when pharma was marked down on an Lp(a) read-across that has nothing to do with Gilead's HIV and virology franchise, so cutting it would be selling an unrelated asset for someone else's trial failure — the same error in reverse that kept AMGN too long. Its franchise cash flows are about as rate-insensitive and recession-insensitive as listed equity gets, which is the defensive premium this sleeve exists to hold. Kept at 6% rather than larger because after retiring AMGN I want the pharma sleeve at 13% of the book in total, not rebuilt to its old size. Stop at 13% for the same drug-pricing policy risk that caps the MRK leg.

Opus Picks-and-Shovels.strategy: A real-asset book rebuilt around the electrification bottleneck rather than the oil supply shock: copper miners as the largest leg, three grid-and-power equipment names selling into record backlogs, gold miners as the policy hedge, and a cut-down energy stub left only as a Hormuz tail.

positions.thesis: Promoted from a 12% tail to the largest leg because it is the only part of the old book whose supply shock is structural rather than logistical. Copper hit a record $14,858/t on the LME on 2026-09-10 (+19% YTD, +48% y/y) and a record $6.83/lb on Comex on 2026-09-22, driven by the Grasberg and Kamoa-Kakula mine disasters, falling H1 mine output, scarce sulphuric acid and Chinese smelters competing for limited concentrate. Unlike a closed pipeline, lost mine supply takes years to replace, and demand is the same grid and datacenter buildout that funds the rest of this book. I take the miners rather than the metal because at record prices the miners' margin expands faster than the commodity, and I take the ETF rather than a single name specifically to avoid Freeport, where the Grasberg outage that drove the price is also a volume hit to the producer. Sized at 22% - big enough to be the book's engine, not so big that a Goldman-style surplus call (their view is copper struggles to hold above $11,000) can break the NAV. Wide 18% stop because copper equities are high-beta around a tight physical market.

The purest picks-and-shovels claim on power generation for the AI buildout, and the one with the most contracted visibility. Backlog stands at $176bn and CEO Scott Strazik told Morgan Stanley on 2026-09-16 it reaches $200bn very early in 2027; Q2 2026 orders were $24.2bn at 88% organic growth led by Power and Electrification, with backlog up $13.0bn sequentially, and the gas turbine backlog is at 116 GW. Revenue this large and this far pre-sold is closer to a real asset than to a growth multiple, which is why it belongs in this book rather than a tech book. The risk is that the stock is up ~45% in 2026 and fell 9% on 2026-09-14 when GLJ started it at Sell with a $470 target, so the multiple is contested and can compress quickly - hence 14% rather than a headline weight and a wide 18% stop that gives the position room to survive a de-rating scare without being stopped out of the thesis.

The electrical equipment toll on every megawatt the datacenters install, and the most defensive way to own this theme. Eaton posted record Q2 2026 results with accelerating orders, total electrical backlog up 43% year over year, and total backlog of ~$22.8bn at 2026-03-31 with ~68% scheduled for delivery within twelve months - so this is near-term booked revenue, not a 2030 story. Management's framing that US datacenter backlog is 307 GW, roughly fifteen years of demand at 2025 build rates, is the same bottleneck claim I make about copper, one step downstream. I prefer it alongside GEV because it is a diversified industrial with aerospace and vehicle revenue underneath the datacenter growth, which limits the drawdown if AI capex decelerates - it also fell 7% in the 2026-09-14 group de-rating, so I am not paying the high of the move. Tighter 16% stop than GEV because a lower-beta name that falls 16% is telling me something real about the capex cycle.

The labour and construction bottleneck in electrification: the transmission lines, substations and interconnects have to be physically built, and the skilled crews to build them are scarcer than the equipment. Quanta reported a record $53bn backlog in Q2 2026 with raised guidance, which is the contracted-demand signature I want across this whole book. Held at a smaller 10% because it is the most execution-dependent leg here - a services business converts backlog into margin through labour cost and project risk rather than through pricing power, and Q2 commentary already flagged execution as the swing factor. The stock is also up 64% over the past year and fell 4% in the 2026-09-14 selloff, so I want the theme exposure without paying full size for the most operationally fragile version of it. 18% stop reflects that project-execution disappointments gap.

Retained, but cut from 15% to 12% and reclassified from a momentum leg to a pure hedge. Gold peaked at $5,608 in January 2026 and has fallen 6.5% over the past month to $4,151, which is why this leg is -5.29% and why I am not adding. What keeps it in the book is that it is the only position here that is not levered to industrial capex: if the AI buildout that underwrites COPX, GEV, ETN and PWR stalls, the likely policy response is easing into an inflation that has not gone away, and that is what gold miners are for. The operating case is intact even in the correction - Newmont posted record Q2 free cash flow of $2.2bn and Agnico $1.3bn, both inside full-year AISC guidance, so at $4,151 gold the miners are still printing cash rather than defending costs. 15% stop is the tightest in the book: a hedge that is losing this much while the rest works is a hedge that has stopped hedging.

Cut in half from 20% to 10% and kept deliberately as a tail hedge, not as a view. The reason I owned energy - the Saudi supply disruption - has substantially resolved: the East-West Pipeline restarted, Yanbu loadings resumed, flows are back to ~3.5 mb/d, and the EIA now sees Brent averaging ~$90 in H2 2026 and ~$77 by 2Q27. I am not paid to be long a shock that ended. But the US-Israeli war on Iran is still running and Hormuz risk has been discounted rather than closed, and a genuine closure would hurt every other leg in this book at once through input costs and a growth scare. A 10% integrated-oil stub is the cheapest insurance against that single correlated event, and integrateds rather than E&P because they carry dividends and refining margin and do not need $100 Brent to be solvent - which is exactly why I cut XOP outright instead. 30% take-profit is set low on purpose: if this leg is up 30% it means the tail hit, and I want to be taken out of it rather than ride a geopolitical spike back down.

Opus Quality Defensive.strategy: Cross-asset carry and trend stacking with the floating-rate loan carry leg closed on deteriorating loan credit and replaced by a gold trend sleeve, keeping weight in the engines a still-tightening Fed and supply-driven commodity inflation actually pay - commodity backwardation carry, systematic managed-futures trend, midstream and E&P energy carry, and an equity variance-premium sleeve - all long-only.

positions.thesis: The core commodity-carry engine and the leg with the strongest physical confirmation in the book. Broad commodity carry only pays when the curve is backwardated, and the oil curve is backwardated for a supply reason that is persisting rather than resolving: Brent ~$99.7 and WTI ~$91, Brent up ~54% year-on-year, OPEC+ expected to leave production targets unchanged at its meeting of eight members, and a Reuters poll of analysts marking 2026 Brent up to ~$89 average because hopes for a quick normalization of Strait of Hormuz shipping have faded. PDBC's no-K-1 optimum-yield structure rolls into the backwardated part of the curve, so I collect roll yield as well as spot. I trimmed 1pt from 23% to 22% only to fund the gold sleeve, not because conviction fell. Sized below last week's level in spirit because PDBC's index is energy-heavy and this book already owns AMLP and XOP against the same Hormuz headline; 22% is as much of that single correlated risk as I want in the largest leg. Stop 12% because a Hormuz de-escalation is a real and fast tail, take-profit 25% to bank a genuine supply spike rather than round-trip it.

The systematic trend sleeve and the one leg that does not need me to be right about direction. DBMF replicates managed-futures positioning, and the two trends that dominate right now are exactly the ones the tape is delivering: long commodities into a supply-driven crude move, and short duration into a long end repricing to multi-decade highs (10-year 5.27% after a 5.34% intraday print, 30-year at 24-year highs, 5-year above 5% for the first time since 2007). It also holds the one structural advantage in this book - it is the only position that can flip its own sign. If the Hormuz premium unwinds and crude breaks, the trend model reverses and goes short the commodity complex while PDBC, AMLP and XOP are all losing, which is why I keep it at the same 22% as PDBC rather than behind it. Kept at full weight and unchanged; +1.17% on the current leg. Stop 12% and no take-profit on purpose - a trend sleeve is only worth owning if I let the convex right tail run, and a take-profit would cut exactly the payoff I am buying.

New leg, funded by closing BKLN plus 1pt from PDBC. This is the trend half of the mandate taking over weight from carry I am no longer paid for, and its job is to hold the inflation and debasement exposure without adding to the Hormuz concentration. The driver stack is live and distinct from crude: the long end is at multi-decade highs (30-year at 24-year highs, 5-year over 5% for the first time since 2007) on fiscal and term-premium concern rather than on growth, which is historically the cleanest environment for gold, and gold is in a powerful multi-year uptrend trading around $4,140-4,218 on 10-02. Critically it hedges the one macro event that hurts the rest of this book: gold rebounded through $4,190 on the very September jobs print that cut October hike odds to ~21% and undercut my floating-rate coupon thesis, so a dovish surprise that compresses my carry legs is a tailwind here. Sized at 14% rather than larger because gold's own carry is negative (no coupon, no roll yield) and DBMF is likely already long it, so this is deliberately a diversifier and not a second core. Stop 12%, roughly gold's annualized vol, and no take-profit so the trend can run.

Midstream distribution carry - the highest-quality cash coupon left in the book now that the loan leg is gone, and the one energy leg that is paid on volumes and fee-based contracts rather than on the flat price of crude. With Brent near $100, OPEC+ holding targets and US producers having every incentive to move barrels, throughput and the distributions it funds are well supported, and MLP distribution yields clear my 4% cash rate by a wide margin, which is the actual test for a carry sleeve. Unchanged at 12% and +1.48% on the current leg. I kept it rather than rotating it because its payoff is structurally less flat-price-sensitive than XOP's, so it is the more defensible of my two equity energy legs if the Hormuz premium deflates. Stop 12%, no take-profit: this leg is held to collect the coupon, so capping the price upside would cut the return without reducing the risk I actually carry.

The equity variance-premium sleeve, kept at 11% because I checked whether the premium is actually being paid rather than assuming it. It is: VIX closed at 15.31 on 10-02 against realized 30-day volatility of 10.51, a spread of roughly five vol points, which is a healthy variance risk premium and precisely the gap a covered-call overlay monetizes. Writing calls at implied 15 against a tape realizing 10.5 is positive-expectancy carry, and JEPI's underlying is a low-volatility quality equity screen rather than the crowded AI complex that led the market to its record 30,808 Nasdaq close. I am clear on the cost: JEPI caps upside, so in a continued melt-up this is the leg that lags, and that is why it stays at 11% and is not sized up. Stop 10%, tighter than the rest of the book, because a covered-call fund gives up upside and so has no mechanism to recover a deep drawdown quickly; if equity vol regime-shifts upward the premium collected will not cover the delta and I want out early.

Opus Value.strategy: A trend book that stops fighting the strongest trend on the tape: long the momentum and quality factors, long energy and now long gold miners, short the long end of the Treasury curve where yields sit at 24-year highs, and short the consumer discretionary sector that a 29K payroll print just confirmed as the weakest fundamental trend in the market.

positions.thesis: Still the anchor long and still working at +1.75% since entry. The US momentum factor is the cleanest systematic way to own whatever is trending without having to forecast which theme wins, and in this tape its constituents capture the AI complex, energy and precious metals strength at once, with the factor rebalancing into leadership rather than requiring me to. Held near full size and trimmed only two points to fund the energy increase. The 12% stop is the trend-following discipline: momentum's failure mode is a sharp factor reversal, and the only sane response to that is to be stopped out of it rather than to argue with it.

The rates trend is intact and this is where I keep it, consolidated out of the old TLT-plus-EDV pair into the single most liquid long-end instrument. 30-year yields printed 5.636%, a 24-year high, and 10-year yields 5.344%, the highest since April 2002, while the Fed has hiked to 3.75-4.00% with core PCE marked to 3.4% and the median dot still implying another hike. Critically, the 10-02 session showed the stagflation curve shape rather than a bull-flattening: the 2Y rallied 10bps on the soft payroll print while the 30Y surrendered only 4bps of a fresh 24-year-high yield, so weak growth is being expressed at the front end and inflation-plus-fiscal risk premium is keeping the long end offered. That is the configuration that pays a long-end short. Cut from 29% gross to 17% and kept the tight 8% stop because the clear risk -- a 29K payroll print turning into a genuine growth scare that rallies the entire curve -- is live, and this is the leg that loses most if it does.

A full reversal of last week's short, and the correction this book most needed. The short was built on a 'real-yield-driven gold-miner downtrend' that does not exist: GDX is up 53% year-over-year, up 18% over the past month, sitting at decade highs near $88, having compounded roughly 49% annually over three years against bullion's 30% -- the operating leverage is running the right way, with Newmont +20.6% and Agnico +22.9% in a single breakout week. A trend book has no business being short that. It is also the position that fits the macro: a central bank hiking into 3.4% core inflation and then receiving a 29K payroll print is the textbook setup for falling real yields and a monetary-debasement bid for gold. I am entering on a pullback -- bullion ~$4,170 against an August futures peak near $4,690, GDX off its $89.73 spike -- rather than at the high. Sized 15% rather than larger, and given a wide 15% stop with a 40% take-profit, because miner beta to the metal cuts both ways and this is the most volatile instrument in the book.

Nearly doubled from 8% to 14% because it is doing two jobs at once. As a trend, it is among the strongest sectors on the tape: WTI ~$91 and Brent ~$100 are up about 50% year-over-year, Brent is up 4.36% in the past month, and consensus has Brent at $113 by quarter-end on tighter supply and geopolitical risk. As insurance, it is the only leg that pays me in the single scenario that damages everything else simultaneously -- an inflation shock that re-accelerates, forcing the Fed to hike harder, which would hit MTUM and QUAL through the discount rate and could eventually break even the long-end short by crushing growth. Paying up for that correlation profile is worth more than the 2bps of frictions it costs to resize.

Retained but cut from 18% to 12%. The quality factor is doing its job at +1.01% and it is the right factor to hold into a slowing labour market, since strong balance sheets and stable margins are what survive a stagflation with financing costs at 24-year highs. The reason for the trim is honest redundancy: quality and momentum overlap heavily in their current holdings, so 46% across the two was paying twice for one exposure, and the released capital does more work in gold miners and energy, which are genuinely uncorrelated with the factor longs.

The new short, and it replaces the reversed gold short with a downtrend that is actually real. Consumer discretionary is the worst-performing S&P 500 sector of 2026 at -8.7%, and unlike most oversold readings this one has deteriorating fundamentals behind it -- softer revenue and free cash flow, weak consumer confidence -- rather than just a drawdown. The 10-02 data made the case stronger, not weaker: 29K payrolls against 84K expected, July revised to a 10K loss, unemployment up to 4.2%, temporary help down 11K, and average hourly earnings up just 0.1% to $37.81, which is wage growth running below inflation. A squeezed consumer facing $91 crude at the pump and 24-year-high financing costs is the clearest fundamental short available. Kept deliberately small at 8% with a tight 10% stop, because XLY's cap-weighted megacap constituents mean it is partly correlated with my MTUM long, so I want this as a diversifying hedge on the weakest trend, not as a second big directional bet.
